notes.meaning: After the shipwreck, everyone reached land, just as God had promised Paul that no one would die. They learned the island was Malta, which lies south of Sicily, between Sicily and Africa. God brought them through safely, not the sailors' skill.

The islanders spoke neither Greek nor Latin, so outsiders called them "barbarians." That word was not an insult. They showed "no ordinary" kindness, building a fire and welcoming every soaked, shivering survivor in the cold rain. God can turn strangers into friends. Their kindness is an example for us to help people in trouble.

Paul, the most important man there, pitched in and gathered sticks like a servant. A viper had been sleeping in the wood for the winter. The heat woke it, and it clamped onto his hand. Danger can meet us even while we are doing good, but God's people always come through to a good end.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that Malta has no poisonous snakes today. They suggest it may have been a harmless look-alike snake that clings and bites. Others answer that vipers simply died out as the island became crowded and farmed.

notes.meaning: The islanders saw the snake hanging from Paul's hand. They may also have seen his chains. They decided he must be a murderer whom the goddess "Justice" would not let escape. They were right that God punishes evil. But they were wrong to think every trouble proves someone guilty, the same mistake Job's friends made. Good people often suffer to test and grow their faith.

Paul calmly shook the snake into the fire and was not hurt. This fulfilled Jesus' promise that his followers would "take up serpents" (Mark 16:18). God had promised Paul would reach Rome, and a snake could not stop that. Faith did not make Paul careless, but it kept fear from ruling him.

The islanders waited for Paul to swell up or drop dead. When nothing happened, they swung to the other extreme and called him a god, just as the crowd at Lystra once had (Acts 14). People's opinions are fickle. Paul was neither a murderer nor a god, but a man of God.

Publius held the title "chief man" of the island, the official name for the island's top Roman officer. Stone inscriptions found on Malta use the same title, which shows how carefully Luke wrote. Publius kindly hosted them for three days. It is a fine thing when God gives a large heart along with a large estate.

Publius's father was in bed with fevers that kept coming back and with dysentery, a serious illness of the bowels. Paul prayed and then laid his hands on him, and he was healed. By praying first, Paul showed that God did the healing and Paul was only His servant. The healing was also God's reward for Publius's kindness.

News spread, and sick people from all over the island kept coming during those months and were cured. Paul did good wherever God placed him, and he very likely shared the gospel along with the healings. Paul was a prisoner, but God's power was not. Some think Luke, the doctor, also helped care for the sick.

The grateful islanders honored Paul and his friends in many ways, likely including gifts. They loaded the ship with supplies for the trip. This was not payment for miracles, since Paul gave freely. It was thanks it would have hurt them to have refused. An old tradition says the church on Malta began with this visit.

After three winter months they sailed on another grain ship from Alexandria that had waited out the winter at Malta. Its figurehead was Castor and Pollux, twin gods that sailors believed protected them. Paul did not choose this ship. Sailing under an idol's sign did not stain him, because he gave the idol no honor.
Their first stop was Syracuse, the chief city of Sicily, about eighty miles from Malta. They stayed three days, perhaps waiting for the wind or doing ship's business.
The ship worked its way around to Rhegium at the toe of Italy. A day later a friendly south wind came up. The next day they reached Puteoli near Naples, the main port for grain ships headed to Rome.

At Puteoli they found fellow Christians who begged them to stay a week. This probably gave Paul a Sunday of worship with them. The centurion kindly allowed it. God has people in places we would never expect. Luke's words "and so we came to Rome" mark the high point of the whole book.

Christians in Rome heard Paul was coming. Some walked out as far as the Forum of Appius, around forty or fifty miles, and others to the Three Taverns, to greet him. Paul had long wanted to see them. Seeing them, he thanked God and took courage. When friends are kind to us, God put it in their hearts, and the fellowship of believers strengthens us.

In Rome, Paul was not thrown into the common jail. He was allowed to live on his own, chained to a soldier who guarded him. This favor likely came from the centurion's good report. Because the guards changed often, many soldiers heard about Christ (Philippians 1:13). God can give His prisoners favor with those who hold them.

Paul was chained and could not go to the synagogue, so he invited the Jewish leaders to come to him. As always, he went to his own people first. He told them he had done nothing against the Jewish people or their customs. Yet he had been handed over to the Romans. Even after so much cruel treatment, he still reached out to them gently.

The Roman officials who examined him, Felix, Festus and King Agrippa, found nothing deserving death and wanted to set him free. It was to Paul's honor that those who looked most carefully at his case found him innocent.

When the Jewish leaders opposed his release, Paul had to appeal to Caesar to save his life. He made clear he had come to defend himself, not to accuse his nation. He spoke gently, never mentioning their plots to kill him, and held no grudge.

Paul said he wore his chain because of "the hope of Israel." This is the hope of the Messiah, God's promised King, and of the dead being raised. He preached that this Messiah had come in Jesus and that his kingdom is spiritual. Real hope looks to Christ.

The leaders said no letters or bad reports about Paul had come from Judea. They were probably telling the truth. Paul's accusers may have seen their case as hopeless after so many judges cleared him. Or news simply could not reach Rome before Paul did.

They wanted to hear Paul's views, since they knew this "sect" (a breakaway group) was spoken against everywhere. Christianity is not a narrow party but is meant for all people. Yet it has always been spoken against. Being opposed is no proof a cause is bad.

On the set day, many came to Paul's lodging. From morning to evening, he explained the kingdom of God. He showed it is spiritual, not an earthly political kingdom. He worked to persuade them that Jesus is the promised Messiah, using the Law of Moses and the Prophets. He built everything on Scripture, showing that the Old and New Testaments agree.

Some were convinced, but others refused to believe. The gospel has always had this double effect. It brings life to those who believe and judgment to those who refuse. Even Paul's skill could not win everyone, so we should not be surprised when people resist today.

As they argued among themselves and started to leave, Paul gave one last solemn word. He said the Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah to their ancestors. Saying the Holy Spirit spoke the words shows that Isaiah's message came from God. Paul had been gentle all day, but now he spoke sharply to the stubborn.

Paul quoted Isaiah 6, a passage Jesus also used. The people heard and saw but did not understand, because their hearts had grown hard and they had shut their own eyes. Otherwise they would turn to God and be healed. Their own stubbornness and God's just judgment worked together. Anyone who hears the gospel and ignores it should take this warning seriously.

differ.view: This blindness comes by God's just judgment and His free choice. Those chosen for life believe, while others stay hard, yet the blame is still their own.
This hardening is God's judgment that follows people's own stubborn refusal of the truth. First they would not believe, and afterward they could not.

notes.meaning: Paul declared that God's salvation has been sent to the Gentiles (non-Jewish people), and they will listen. He had said this twice before (Acts 13:46; 18:6). The Jews could not complain when others took the gift they had pushed away. Paul hoped it would stir them to jealousy so some would still turn (Romans 11:14). Paul never gave up on spreading the gospel.

This verse is missing from the oldest manuscripts and was probably added later. It says the Jews left arguing hard among themselves. Many people argue without reasoning rightly. Only God's grace opens a person's understanding. It is not the gospel but contempt for the gospel that causes such strife.

For two full years Paul lived in a rented house, still under guard, and welcomed everyone who came, Jews or Gentiles. His case probably waited because his accusers did not come. During this time he likely wrote Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon. His prison became a church, and God's word could not be chained.

Boldly and with no one stopping him, Paul preached the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ. These two go together, because the kingdom rests on what Christ did to save us. Acts ends with the gospel freely preached in the capital of the world. Early Christians believed Paul was later released and finally died as a martyr under Nero.
